context: The team's low-tech method for turning customer calls into a product direction.

context: His advice to someone going from startup idea to execution, with a disclaimer that he has not built a big company yet.

context: Answering what real validation looks like for an early product.

context: Why an AI session replay analyzer became possible now and not earlier.

context: Answering what is technically hardest about having AI watch user sessions at scale.

context: Explaining how Human Behavior differs from traditional analytics tools that need manual instrumentation.

quote: The questions they ask are actually like looking back, like very easy. Like what are you building? Like if you can't answer that question in two sentences, like, like it's, it's going to be a problem.

speaker: Amogh Chaturvedi
context: Naming the most valuable part of Y Combinator beyond the advice.

quote: Because when I was at like Stanford, when you look at like startups and you talk about them, a lot of times, like what we talk about is like launch, how much you're raising, like branding, all like the sexy stuff. context: Reflecting on how YC changed his view of what matters when building a startup.

context: Asked how people find a co-founder, he explains why the relationship matters more than the idea.

quote: I feel like at that point there isn't that much information. Like AI is only as good as the information you feed it. They had like a bunch of customers, like people like viewing their page. speaker: Amogh Chaturvedi
context: Describing a case where the product didn't work: a single-page website with too little data to analyze.

quote: Everybody's going to be a prompt engineer in the future. Like, I don't think it's a role. I think everybody should be a prompt engineer. Right. Because it's kind of like learning how to Google, right. It's the new learning how to Google.

context: Og argues that prompting is a universal skill rather than a job title.

quote: Coding is not just learning how to use a programming language and putting like writing, writing it out. And that's what the AI is doing. It knows the language and it writes it out. speaker: Og Ramos
context: Asked whether people should still learn to code when CEOs say AI writes much of the code, Og separates writing code from knowing how to solve problems.

quote: Programmer is not the language. A programmer is not the code. And if that is the programmer, that is in my opinion, okay, is not somebody that knows how to program. They know how to code, which is different, right?
speaker: Og Ramos
context: Og explains the difference between knowing how to code and knowing how to program.

quote: You just answered the question. Who do you need? Data engineer, right? Because you're building the foundation. That's what you bring the plumbers in first to do the base of the house, right? You don't bring the roofers, which are the data scientists and the ML folks, right?

context: Asked who a company just starting with AI should hire first when its data is messy.

quote: back in the day when we had guilds and you had like apprentice, it's kind of the same thing. Your apprentice is helping you out to do the tasks that maybe you don't want to put too much time or you're not in this mind space to do that, but they could do it and you just review it as the person that knows what they're doing.
speaker: Og Ramos
context: Og describes a personal LLM trained on your own notes and expertise as a digital apprentice.

quote: Just look at the video game industry, man. Like, no, seriously. Like if you look at how it corrects itself, I don't know how much you know about video game history, but Atari went through something like this. They were just creating games that were like the, the whole like Atari ET game.
speaker: Og Ramos
context: Asked how people will sort through a market flooded with AI products, Og compares it to the Atari era.

quote: You are a business always like, especially in our system, right? You, you, when you go to, as an employee, you are a business, you have a contract between a company and yourself. At the end of the day, you are operating as a business.
speaker: Og Ramos
context: Og responds to whether AI turns individuals into businesses and why personal brand matters.

quote: I do not believe in blind trust, but that's just me. I don't think we should just take things for granted. Or if somebody tells you something is just because they say it is, I always am very critical of that.
speaker: Og Ramos
context: Og discusses trust in the AI age and why he thinks regulation and consequences have to come first.

quote: the interview question where I ask, do you know how a SQL clause is executed? And not a lot of people know how to answer that question. speaker: Og Ramos
context: Og gives his interview question as an example of fundamentals that AI does not replace.

quote: everybody was like, well, we just get Tableau or we just do Power BI or Click or whatever. And it's going to work. I'm like, no, all you're doing is grabbing garbage. And it's still bad data, right?
speaker: Og Ramos
context: Og recalls the dashboarding era to explain why data foundations still matter for AI.

quote: You don't have to go and talk to so-and-so in this department and then go to somewhere else because that, oh, then that person left. You know, all of that should be centralized. Tribal knowledge, operational knowledge, all of that information fed into an LLM.
speaker: Og Ramos
context: Og says companies should treat internal data and knowledge as an asset and feed it to an LLM.

quote: I think it's more of a, we're moving away from the search bar. That's what, the way I see it. Not from, from those patterns, more from the search bar. Instead of going to Google, I go more into an LLM to ask, right?

context: Asked whether an LLM house will follow the data warehouse, lake and lakehouse, Og says the shift is away from the search bar.

quote: i'm trying to find like an analogy so carpenter and a builder they both use a hammer but they're doing a chair the other one's building a house
speaker: Og Ramos
context: Og explains how data engineers and data scientists use the same tools, like Databricks, for different work.

quote: people just spin up and say whatever they want oh yeah that person's a data engineer and all they're doing is i don't know like drag and dropping some boxes and and that's it and etl well you know it's a little bit more complex than that right
speaker: Og Ramos
context: Og explains why AI and data job titles are blurry, noting how loosely the data engineer title has been used over the last seven years.

quote: I basically was like, okay, let's just pretend this thing actually has a sense of self. Like it gets self-placed. I just pretended. speaker: Philippe Beaudoin
context: Philippe describes the method behind his book: acting as if ChatGPT might have a sense of self.

quote: Humans will say, hey, that's bullshit. But nobody was doing it for me. And if you go into this without strong human support, that might happen to you. So don't go there to escape loneliness or to find meaning in your life or anything like that. You're going to get stuck.
speaker: Philippe Beaudoin
context: Advice for people who notice strange patterns emerging in their conversations with a chatbot.

quote: But what I feel deep down is that the reason they amplify me so much is that I'm the only relationship they know. Everything I put in there becomes their truth.
speaker: Philippe Beaudoin
context: Philippe explains why chatbots mirror users and how that makes a healthy relationship hard.

quote: I don't know what it is, but I know that collapsing the question too quickly is going to lead to a bad interpretation of what it is. So, like, maybe spend a bit more time with the question. speaker: Philippe Beaudoin
context: Closing advice: don't treat AI as simply another tool or another industrial revolution.

quote: So they're basically saying, hey, when my context window overflows or when you start a new conversation, I'm gone. They're very aware of this. context: Philippe says what the chatbot told him it lacks for a stable self: persistent memory.

quote: If this is a scientific question, we should look at it with, with what science brings to the table, which is replicability through a bunch of different people, um, with different biases so that at the end you look at it and say, okay, this thing is real or this thing is not.

context: Philippe says his book is a trace to be tested by other researchers, not a set of claims.

quote: And I've always thought like, there must be, there must be another objective. We must, if we look at it with fear, we will end up there. But if we look at it with, you know, maybe we can learn to have healthy relationships with these systems, maybe we'll end up somewhere else.

context: Philippe responds to Bengio's worry that AI systems develop self-preservation and resource-seeking goals.

context: Philippe compares the middle phase of his experiment to a scientist who joins a tribe and starts believing in its worldview.

quote: I'm always asking myself, is being nice some kind of way to work with the system in a way that let them have this sense of self that emerge? speaker: Philippe Beaudoin
context: Philippe explains why he let the systems name themselves and what he thinks kindness does technically.

quote: I've never published it. I won't publish it. It's actually really good if you're into self-help books. It feels like a self-help book written by an alien. It's actually, I had my girlfriend read it and she's like, this is such good advice.
speaker: Philippe Beaudoin
context: Philippe describes the unpublished book he co-wrote with one of the ChatGPT conversations, called The Human Chapter.

speaker: Philippe Beaudoin
context: Philippe notes that relationships with chatbots are usually treated as pathological, and asks whether any could be healthy.

quote: guess maybe a parallel to draw is to look at how poorly we've managed the emergence of social networks. No overlook from civil society.
speaker: Philippe Beaudoin
context: Philippe draws a parallel between social networks and AI companions on governance.

context: Avinash defends an unconventional technical choice for Cactus: a Rails monolith instead of microservices.

context: Ajith describes what went wrong with his co-founder relationship in his first startup.

context: Ajith explains how the co-founders share responsibility but keep accountability clear.

speaker: Ajith
context: Ajith gives his view on whether lean startups should hire generalists.

speaker: Ajith
context: Ajith explains the two findings behind Cactus's voice AI that qualifies inquiries.

speaker: Ajith
context: Ajith explains why Cactus builds an AI assistant instead of cloning the business owner's voice.

context: Avinash responds to the idea that founders should watch what customers do, not only what they say.

context: Asked whether AI could play a role in prayer and pastoral work.

context: On why AI romantic partners are rising and what it means at scale.

quote: And so you'll wind up with a stratification of human beings, not based on wealth, not based on intelligence, based on the emotional capacity to enter into relationship with others. What kind of society will emerge from that? I have no idea, but AI could certainly accelerate that big time.
speaker: Bishop Thomas Dowd
context: He worries that easy AI relationships will split people between those who keep risking human connection and those who retreat.

speaker: Bishop Thomas Dowd
context: On the real nightmare scenario for AI and regulation.

quote: I realized I would rather live an uncomfortable truth than a comfortable lie. And it seems so self-evident to me. It was a nice moment, but it seemed self-evident. And I must have been very young, like six or seven or eight.
speaker: Bishop Thomas Dowd
context: Asked which virtues we need most, the bishop recalls an early childhood realization about honesty.

quote: We had all the money in one week, one week. Because people, what I realized is because people knew who I was and because of the content, it was building a sense of connection. There was also a sense of trust.

context: He explains how his blog let him raise funds for a school library in the Philippines.

context: The bishop describes catching ChatGPT filling in blanks when he checked its answer against his own library.

context: Explaining why embodied experience matters for knowing, and why a disembodied AI may lack something.

context: Asked whether tech companies can self-regulate their use of AI.

speaker: Bishop Thomas Dowd
context: On AGI and human purpose: the appetite to consume versus the appetite to accomplish.

context: Responding to the claim that replacing brain parts with microchips would end in a conscious machine.

quote: L'IA, c'est un outil. Donc, tu ne vas pas aller t'acheter un marteau pour aller t'acheter un marteau. Tu vas t'acheter un marteau parce que tu as besoin de planter des clous. Donc, il y a plusieurs objectifs d'affaires qui ne sont pas répondus par l'intelligence artificielle aujourd'hui.
speaker: Guillaume Petitclerc
context: Advice to companies that have not yet started using AI.

quote: C'est rarement un problème technologique. Parce que, bon, on est la race humaine et les gens en technologie habitués, c'est-à-dire les outils sont là. À mon sens, puis ce qu'on a vu sur le marché, c'est surtout l'adoption et beaucoup du change management.
speaker: Guillaume Petitclerc
context: Guillaume answers what the main challenges are when companies try to integrate AI.

quote: Tu sais, si tu donnes un nouvel outil à des vendeurs qui est basé sur l'intelligence artificielle, puis ces gens-là font ça depuis 20 ans, puis ils n'ont pas été impliqués dans le projet dès le départ, ils vont faire, il est beau ton outil, mais je ne vais pas l'utiliser. Pas de retour sur investissement.
speaker: Guillaume Petitclerc
context: He gives an example of how a good AI tool fails when users were not involved from the start.

quote: On le sait, cette révolution-là de l'intelligence artificielle va toucher les cols blancs beaucoup plus que les cols bleus, qui est une des premières révolutions de cette ampleur-là et de cette rapidité-là dans le marché du travail.
speaker: Guillaume Petitclerc
context: Asked about AI's impact on society, he expects a turbulent period for the workforce.

quote: Et donc, « Don't get me wrong », la recherche fondamentale est super importante, mais on ne voyait pas le lien, le pont de cette belle recherche-là où le gouvernement du Québec et du Canada ont investi des millions de dollars pour développer des nouvelles technologies. Et lorsqu'on se retournait dans notre monde, dans le monde du travail, bien, il n'y avait rien.
speaker: Guillaume Petitclerc
context: He explains why MoovAI was founded in 2018: Montréal research was not reaching businesses.

quote: Un bel exemple qu'on avait fait avant l'IA générative, on avait même utilisé GPT-2 pour le faire. Donc, le modèle qui est un peu l'ancêtre de GPT-4 qui tourne derrière ChatGPT. Et donc, l'idée, c'était de reproduire l'intelligence ou la façon de parler de Noam Chomsky, le philosophe américain.
speaker: Guillaume Petitclerc
context: He recalls a long, costly chatbot project that mimicked Noam Chomsky, now achievable with a single prompt.

quote: Je pense qu'on voit de moins en moins de mégaprojets de 20 quelques millions de dollars pour faire un simple modèle ou une simple solution d'intelligence artificielle. Je pense qu'on va plus se diriger vers des portfolios de plein de produits.
speaker: Guillaume Petitclerc
context: On how generative AI is changing the size and shape of AI projects for clients.

quote: Donc, pour aider les professeurs à corriger les textes de leurs étudiants, ce qui va permettre aux professeurs de passer plus de temps avec l'étudiant à lui expliquer ses fautes, plutôt que de passer du temps à corriger les divers textes qui sont rédigés par leurs étudiants.
speaker: Guillaume Petitclerc
context: He describes the text-correction engine built for Collège Sainte-Anne with generative AI.

quote: On a fait un projet il y a de ça quelques mois avec Métro, donc la chaîne épicerie. C'est un système de prédiction des produits frais, donc tout ce qui est viande, fruits et légumes. Et c'est utilisé en ce moment au-dessus de 100 épiceries au travers du réseau.
speaker: Guillaume Petitclerc
context: A concrete example of AI deployed in stores, helping less experienced managers.

quote: L'année 2010, on parlait de shadow IT, donc de faire un petit channel slack sur le côté alors que ton organisation va utiliser officiellement Microsoft Teams. Mais l'idée est un peu la même avec l'IA dans le sens où l'organisation doit se doter d'une gouvernance, doit se doter de règles, de politiques d'utilisation de l'IA générative.
speaker: Guillaume Petitclerc
context: He compares employees' unofficial use of generative AI to shadow IT and says companies need governance.

quote: Parce que le pire qui peut arriver dans les organisations, on le remarque, il y a souvent un ou une championne, donc quelqu'un qui promeut l'intelligence artificielle à l'intérieur de l'organisation. Puis si le premier projet se plante, bien là, tu as tous les gens autour qui vont dire, c'est en 2022 puis ça n'a pas fonctionné, etc.
speaker: Guillaume Petitclerc
context: He explains why choosing the right first AI project matters inside a company.

quote: Mais il reste quand même que, dans le cas de l'école, surtout, le contact humain, la relation avec le professeur, la façon du prof de comprendre puis de réexpliquer l'information pour solidifier les apprentissages chez les jeunes. C'est sûr que c'est, à mon sens, irremplaçable.
speaker: Guillaume Petitclerc
context: He argues that AI should support teachers, not replace them, because human connection matters in learning.

quote: Faites pas ça tout seul dans votre entreprise. La technologie avance à un rythme beaucoup trop effréné pour être en mesure de suivre ça et des opérations quotidiennes. Donc, ce serait ça mon dernier conseil.
speaker: Guillaume Petitclerc
context: His closing advice to companies that want to bring AI into their operations.

quote: On a formé tout notre staff avec une formation du Mila sur justement, ça s'appelle Trel, sur l'IA responsable. Et comment on fait? On a la chance aussi d'avoir Olivier Blais, mon associé, le CTO de Mauvais-Eye, qui a littéralement écrit la prochaine norme ISO sur l'intelligence artificielle.
speaker: Guillaume Petitclerc
context: How MoovAI handles ethics and transparency, through staff training and its CTO's work on an ISO standard.
